title: Why population growth rates differ between countries

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain how and why birth rates, death rates and net migration vary between countries.

blocks.heading: Why birth and death rates differ
blocks.text: Birth rates tend to be higher in low-income countries, where children contribute to household income early and schooling for girls and family planning are harder to reach. In high-income countries such as Germany or Japan, children cost more to raise and educate, and families tend to be small. Death rates follow income and health care: where clinics, clean water and secure food are scarce, more people die young and life expectancy, the average years a newborn would live if the year's pattern of deaths continued, is shorter. Improving healthcare can lower mortality while births remain high, allowing rapid population growth. However, the crude death rate also depends on age structure: an ageing population can have a high rate despite good healthcare.

blocks.heading: Net migration between countries
blocks.text: People move towards work and away from hardship, so the migration side of growth differs widely. Germany draws in workers because its wages and openings are high, while conflict or drought pushes people out of their home countries. Within southern Africa, movement follows mines, ports and harvests: a worker leaving Oshakati for Windhoek shifts the count within the country, whereas leaving for Germany reduces the national count.

blocks.heading: Death rates and net migration: why they differ
blocks.text:
Death rates differ between countries for three main reasons.

Health and living conditions: where clinics, doctors, vaccinations, clean water, sanitation and a secure food supply are within reach, fewer people die of infectious disease and fewer babies and young children die. At a given age, mortality is therefore likely to be higher where these services are scarce; the overall crude death rate also depends on age structure.

Disease and conflict: an epidemic or a war can raise the death rate sharply. In southern Africa, HIV and AIDS pushed death rates up and cut life expectancy in the 1990s and early 2000s, until treatment became widely available.

Age structure: the death rate counts deaths per 1000 of the whole population, so a country with many older people records more deaths even where its health care is excellent. That is why Japan or Germany can record a higher death rate than a poorer country whose population is mostly young.

Net migration differs because of pull and push factors. Pull factors draw people in: jobs, higher wages, safety, good schools and universities, and family already living there. Push factors drive people out: unemployment, low pay, conflict, drought and persecution. Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States record net immigration; within southern Africa, South Africa draws workers from neighbouring countries. Net migration also depends on what limits movement: immigration rules, the cost of travel, and language. A country can have immigrants and emigrants at once - skilled doctors may leave while construction workers arrive - and the net figure is the balance of the two.

blocks.heading: Birth rate or infant mortality rate?
blocks.text: Answers on this objective sometimes swap two measures that sound alike. The birth rate counts live births per 1000 people in a year. The infant mortality rate counts deaths of babies under one per 1000 live births in a year. The boundary: one measures new life against the whole population, the other early deaths against the babies born. The test: ask what is counted and out of what group. A country can have a high birth rate and a falling infant mortality rate together, because better care keeps babies alive without changing how many are born.

blocks.heading: Interest rates and tax rates do not answer it
blocks.text: Some answers drift into policy terms: interest rates, the price a borrower pays a lender for borrowed money, or tax rates, the compulsory share of income or spending taken by the government. The boundary: interest is a price agreed with a lender, whereas a tax is a payment required by law. The test: ask who receives the payment and whether it is compulsory. Neither drives population growth, which turns on the birth rate, the death rate and net migration, so an answer built on borrowing costs has left the question.
